youtube_title: How I Made a Shopify Brand $58k in 90 Days (Without More Traffic)
title: How Two A/B Tests Made a Shopify Brand $58k in 90 Days
meta_title: Shopify A/B Tests: $58k in 90 Days Without More Traffic
meta_description: Two Shopify A/B tests, a real product video in the gallery and a simpler cart drawer, added $58k in 90 days. See the results and how to copy them.
teaser: A real product video and a simpler cart drawer added $58k in 90 days for a Shopify brand, with the same traffic.
summary: We added $58,000 in revenue to a Shopify store in 90 days without extra traffic by running two A/B tests: a real, unpolished product video in slide two or three of the product page gallery, and a stripped-back cart drawer with the delivery time written under the checkout button. The video lifted revenue per visitor by just over 6%, and the simpler cart moved the share of cart viewers reaching checkout from 33% to 38%, lifting revenue per visitor by 11%.
key_takeaways: Start with a conversion autopsy: ask why the visitors you already have drop off, then find the leaking funnel steps (here: product page to add to cart, and cart to checkout).
Add a real video of real hands using the product as slide two or three of your product gallery, and make sure it opens full screen when tapped on mobile.
Open your cart drawer on your phone and count the elements. If there are more than five, you have something to test.
Remove the discount code box from the cart. Shopify's checkout already has one, so nobody loses the option, and you stop sending people to Google looking for codes.
Show each price once (old and new price on the line item) and rewrite upsells to say why customers buy them instead of calling them a no-brainer.
Put your delivery time in one line directly under the checkout button to remove the last doubt before checkout.
A/B test every change until it reaches statistical significance, because what works for one brand does not always work for another.

sections.heading: How did two A/B tests add $58k to a Shopify store without more traffic?

blocks.text: We made one of our clients **$58,000 in 90 days** by changing two simple things on their Shopify store. No extra traffic, no new ads. One change was on the product page, the other in the cart drawer.

A quick note on how we get to that number. We run every test until it reaches **statistical significance**: the point where the data is so sure that if you ran the exact same test again, you would see the same result. So there's no noise in it.
We measure the uplift in revenue, not only conversion rate. Then we extrapolate that uplift to three months to get a ballpark of how much extra revenue the changes actually generated for the client.

sections.heading: Where should you start: more traffic or a conversion autopsy?

blocks.text: The store already had thousands of visitors. So we started where we always start, with a **conversion autopsy**. Instead of asking how to get more people to the site, we ask why the people who already come there drop off. There are always elements of frustration, or things that are simply not clear.
After looking at the data we found two leaks in the funnel:

items: Lots of people reached the product page but didn't add to cart.
People who did add to cart didn't reach checkout.

blocks.text: So we made one change on each of those two steps.

sections.heading: Why weren't the polished product photos selling?

blocks.text: This brand sells puzzles. Customers aren't buying a finished object. They're buying an experience through a physical product: two nights of entertainment, away from screens, focused on themselves and a puzzle in front of them. That is the experience the shopper needs to feel.

When we came in, the product page looked perfect: high quality images, perfect lighting, everything clean. But it was **clean and cold**. That creates a gap. When people buy, they want to know what's in it for them and to experience the product before they buy it. Whatever you sell, they need to be able to imagine what they're like with that product.
If your page doesn't give them that, they go looking for it elsewhere, on YouTube for example, or they leave the site and never come back.

sections.heading: What happens when you add a real video to the product gallery?

blocks.text: We added **a real video to the image gallery**: real hands, a real user playing around with the product. That shows people what the product is actually like far better than polished pictures do.

items: It sits right in the gallery, as image two or three.
On mobile the gallery is even smaller, so once someone taps it, it must play full screen.
Everything else stayed the same: same price, same product. Only the way it's conveyed changed.

blocks.text: We ran it as an A/B test: half the traffic saw the old version, half saw the new one, for a set amount of time, until we knew which performed best. The result: **conversion rate up almost 6% and revenue per visitor up slightly more than 6%**.

That sounds small, but with thousands of visitors and orders it makes a huge impact. And because it's on the product page, which everybody who makes a purchase sees, it's fair to say the site's revenue went up by about 6% without spending more on ads.

sections.heading: Why does a cart drawer with too many elements lose sales?

blocks.text: The product page test was the smaller one. The cart test had **double the impact**, and it came from doing less.

At first glance the old cart drawer looked fine. It had a free shipping bar, upsells, savings, payment icons: everything a good cart is supposed to have. And every cart app you install will happily sell you one more thing to add.

But count what it asks a shopper to read: **eight things in a drawer people see for about 10 seconds**. The person in the cart has already decided they want it. The cart's only job is to get them to checkout without giving them a reason to stop. This cart gave them a few:

items: A discount box sends people to Google looking for a code. Some never come back.
Savings shown twice starts to feel like a sales pitch.

sections.heading: What should you remove, keep and add in your Shopify cart?

blocks.text: We removed every element that wasn't used or relevant on this store, kept what earns its place, and added one line.

items: **Removed the discount box.** People are still asked for discount codes at checkout.
**Removed the savings summary.** The saving now appears only on the product line item, as the old price next to the new price.
**Kept the upsell, but rewrote it.** Instead of calling it a no-brainer, it now says customers use X, which adds a bit of social proof, plus a line explaining what the add-on is actually for.
**Added delivery details under the checkout button.** One line: the product arrives in 6 to 8 days, or whatever your dates are.

blocks.text: That delivery line repeats something already communicated earlier on the site. But it's exactly what the customer is wondering about in the cart, and removing that doubt is the cart's job.

sections.heading: How much did the simpler cart improve conversion?

blocks.text: Before the change, **33% of shoppers who saw the cart reached checkout. After, it was 38%.** That higher conversion pushed revenue per visitor up by 11%.

Average order value didn't change. That's fine: as long as revenue per visitor goes up, we're good. In this case it worked out to **$3 more for every visitor who opens the cart**, which over thousands of users is very significant revenue.
Most people say you need to add more, more, more, but we did the opposite. We made it simpler.
Add the product page win and the cart win together and you get almost $60,000 in additional revenue from very simple changes.

sections.heading: How can you copy these two changes on your own Shopify store?

blocks.text: Start with the cart, because it's simpler. Open your cart on your phone right now and count the elements. If there are more than five, you have something to test.

items: Move the discount code box to checkout. Shopify's checkout already has one, so nobody loses it.
Rewrite your upsell so it says why people buy it.
Put your delivery time right under the checkout button.

blocks.text: Then the product page. Ask yourself what moment people are really buying. For a kit, it's the build and the reveal. For a jacket, it's how it moves. For skincare, it's the texture on the skin. Film that moment.

items: Filming on a phone is perfectly fine. Real beats polished here.
Put it in slide two or three of your gallery, where people already swipe.
On mobile, make sure tapping it opens full screen. A video nobody can see doesn't sell anything.

blocks.text: Finally, **test it instead of just shipping it**. Things that work for one brand don't always work for another. If you have enough traffic, run it as an A/B test until it reaches statistical significance, so you can prove it actually makes you more money.

sections.heading: Why fix your site before buying more traffic?

blocks.text: Buying traffic is expensive. Improving your site is like reconstructing your house: you need the fundamentals right before you go out and win traffic. When your store converts better, you can afford to buy traffic, and even afford to outbid the competition and steal their lunch.

What these two tests show: communicate a real value proposition and real product information, not something polished and perfect. Once you've said something, let it sit and get out of the way. Don't repeat things, don't clutter, don't make it complicated. Make it simple and seamless for the customer.

faq.q: How can I increase Shopify revenue without more traffic?
faq.a: Run a conversion autopsy to find where your existing visitors drop off, then test fixes on those steps. In the video, one product page test and one cart test added $58,000 in 90 days for a Shopify brand with the same traffic. The gains came from a real product video and a simpler cart drawer.

faq.q: Should I add a video to my Shopify product page gallery?
faq.a: In our test, a real video of real hands using the product, placed as slide two or three of the gallery, lifted conversion rate by almost 6% and revenue per visitor by just over 6%. Film the moment people are actually buying, a phone is fine, and make sure it plays full screen when tapped on mobile.

faq.q: Should I remove the discount code box from my Shopify cart?
faq.a: A discount box in the cart sends people to Google looking for a code, and some never come back. Shopify's checkout already has a discount field, so removing it from the cart doesn't take the option away. It was one of the changes in a cart test that moved checkout reach from 33% to 38%.

faq.q: How many elements should a cart drawer have?
faq.a: Open your cart on your phone and count. If it has more than five different elements, you have something to test. The original cart in the video asked shoppers to read eight things in a drawer they see for about 10 seconds.

faq.q: What should I put under the checkout button in my cart?
faq.a: Add one line with the delivery time, for example that the product arrives in 6 to 8 days. Even if you mention it elsewhere on the site, it's exactly what shoppers wonder about in the cart, and it removes doubt right before checkout.

faq.q: Do I need to A/B test these changes or can I just ship them?
faq.a: Test them. Changes that work for one brand don't always work for another. If you have enough traffic, run an A/B test until it reaches statistical significance so you can prove the change makes you more money.
